claim: Stress granules are non-membrane bound RNA-protein (RNP) assemblies that form when translation initiation is limited.
source: Stress granules are non-membrane bound RNA-protein (RNP) assemblies that form when translation initiation is limited and contain a biphasic structure with stable core structures surrounded by a less concentrated shell.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a defining characteristic of stress granules.

claim: Stress granules contain a biphasic structure with stable core structures surrounded by a less concentrated shell.
source: Stress granules are non-membrane bound RNA-protein (RNP) assemblies that form when translation initiation is limited and contain a biphasic structure with stable core structures surrounded by a less concentrated shell.
evidence: This structural characterization is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Core formation is an early event in granule assembly.
source: Time course analysis of granule assembly suggests that core formation is an early event in granule assembly.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by time-course experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Stress granule disassembly is a stepwise process with shell dissipation followed by core clearance.
source: Stress granule disassembly is also a stepwise process with shell dissipation followed by core clearance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through live cell imaging in Figure 11.

claim: Perturbations that alter liquid-liquid phase separations (LLPS) driven by intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDR) of RNA binding proteins in vitro have the opposite effect on stress granule assembly in vivo.
source: Perturbations that alter liquid-liquid phase separations (LLPS) driven by intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDR) of RNA binding proteins in vitro have the opposite effect on stress granule assembly in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by temperature experiments (Figure 6) and 1,6-Hexanediol experiments (Figures 7-10).

claim: Stress granules are thought to influence mRNA function, localization, and to affect signaling pathways.
source: Stress granules are thought to influence mRNA function, localization, and to affect signaling pathways (Buchan, 2014; Buchan and Parker, 2009; Kedersha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pathological mutations in proteins can increase the formation or decrease the clearance of stress granules.
source: However, pathological mutations in proteins that either increase the formation, or decrease the clearance of stress granules, can lead to abnormal accumulation of aggregates that share components with stress granules (Buchan et al., 2013; Dormann et al., 2010; Izumi et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Abnormal accumulation of stress granule-like aggregates is associated with neurodegenerative disease.
source: Abnormal accumulation of stress granule-like aggregates is associated with neurodegenerative disease (Li et al., 2013; Ramaswami et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Stress granules are thought to represent multicomponent viscous liquid droplets that form spontaneously by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
source: Stress granules are members of an emerging class of non-membrane bound organelles and are thought to represent multicomponent viscous liquid droplets that from spontaneously by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) (Brangwynne, 2013; Brangwynne et al., 2009, 2015; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Hyman and Simons, 2012; Hyman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In vitro LLPS droplets display many properties of in vivo stress granules including fusion, wetting, shearing, and dynamicity.
source: In vitro LLPS droplets display many properties of in vivo stress granules including fusion, wetting, shearing, and dynamicity (Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: LLPS in vitro can be driven by high local concentrations of proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: LLPS in vitro can be driven by high local concentrations of proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015; Nott et al., 2015; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: IDR-containing proteins are enriched in stress granules and other mRNP granules.
source: Since IDR-containing proteins are enriched in stress granules and other mRNP granules (Decker et al., 2007; Gilks et al., 2004; Jain et al., 2016; Kato et al., 2012; King et al., 2012; Reijns et al., 2008), this has led to the suggestion that IDRs on mRNA binding proteins form hetero- and homotypic interactions that drive initial formation of stress granules and P-bodies (Gilks et al., 2004; Decker et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Toretsky and Wright, 2014; Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The interactions amongst IDRs driving phase-separation are enhanced by lower salt concentration, molecular crowding, addition of RNA, or lower temperature.
source: The interactions amongst IDRs driving phase-separation are enhanced by altering the molecular milieu either through lower salt concentration, molecular crowding, addition of RNA, or lower temperature (Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015; Nott et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: 1,6-Hexanediol is hypothesized to perturb weak hydrophobic interactions and disassemble assemblies that exhibit liquid-like properties in vitro.
source: In contrast, small aliphatic molecules, such as 1,6-Hexanediol, are hypothesized to perturb weak hydrophobic interactions, and thus disassemble assemblies that exhibit liquid-like properties in vitro (Patel et al., 2007; Ribbeck and Görlich, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mammalian stress granules have been reported to disassemble when cells are treated with 1,6-Hexanediol.
source: Indeed, since mammalian stress granules have been reported to disassemble when cells are treated with 1,6-Hexanediol, they have been inferred to be LLPSs (Kroschwald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mammalian stress granules are comprised of two phases: a less concentrated shell and more stable internal 'core' structures.
source: Analysis of mammalian stress granules has revealed they are comprised of two phases: a less concentrated shell, which disassembles upon cell lysis and thus behaves like a LLPS formed by weak interactions; and more stable, internal 'core' structures (Jain et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The shell of mammalian stress granules disassembles upon cell lysis and behaves like a LLPS formed by weak interactions.
source: Analysis of mammalian stress granules has revealed they are comprised of two phases: a less concentrated shell, which disassembles upon cell lysis and thus behaves like a LLPS formed by weak interactions; and more stable, internal 'core' structures (Jain et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Formation of in vitro liquid droplets by IDRs have been observed to mature into a second, less dynamic phase comprised in part of stable amyloid-like assemblies.
source: Interestingly, formation of in vitro liquid droplets by IDRs have been observed to mature into a second, less dynamic phase comprised in part of stable amyloid-like assemblies (Han et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2012; Kwon et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Stress granules began to form 13–15 min after NaAsO2 stress induction.
source: We observed that stress granules began to form 13–15 min after stress induction, which correlated with an increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 1B,C, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Stress granule formation correlated with an increase in eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: We observed that stress granules began to form 13–15 min after stress induction, which correlated with an increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 1B,C, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Initial stress granules grew in size both by accretion of material and by fusion with other stress granules.
source: The initial stress granules then grew in size both by accretion of material and by fusion with other stress granules (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The area of GFP-G3BP1 stress granules continued to increase with the majority of stress granule assembly completed by 40 min.
source: The area of GFP-G3BP1 stress granules continued to increase with the majority of stress granule assembly completed by 40 min.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: By 15 min after NaAsO2 induction, when stress granules are first visible in cells, there is an increase in the number of stable stress granule cores detected in lysates.
source: Lysis of cells at 5 min, 10 min, and 15 min after NaAsO2 induction revealed that by 15 min, when stress granules are first visible in cells, we observed an increase in the number of stable stress granule cores detected in lysates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GFP-G3BP1 foci in lysates contain PABP1, poly(A)+ RNA, and eIF4G.
source: We identify these GFP-G3BP1 foci in lysates as stress granule cores since they contain PABP1, poly(A)+ RNA, and eIF4G (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Yeast stress granules are stable in lysates as soon as they are microscopically detectible in vivo.
source: Similarly, yeast stress granules are stable in lysates as soon as they are microscopically detectible in vivo (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: As soon as stress granules are observed in cells by microscopy they contain core assemblies that are stable in lysates.
source: We interpret this observation to indicate that as soon as stress granules are observed in cells by microscopy they contain core assemblies that are stable in lysates.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: Stress granules contained substructure as soon as they were large enough to be examined by SIM (20 min).
source: Using SIM for G3BP1, as assessed by mapping pixel intensity for individual granules, we observed that stress granules contained substructure as soon as they were large enough to be examined by SIM (20 min) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: GFP-G3BP1 granule core size does not significantly change between 15 min, 30 min, 60 min, and 120 min of NaAsO2 stress.
source: By Nanosight Nanoparticle Tracking analysis of lysates from U-2 OS cells at different times after stress, we observed that GFP-G3BP1 granule core size does not significantly change between 15 min (median size, 259 ± 74 nm), 30 min (median size, 258 ± 24 nm), 60 min (median size, 273 ± 12 nm), and 120 min (median size, 247 ± 4 nm) of NaAsO2 stress (one-way ANOVA, p-value = 0.94) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The recovery rates of GFP-G3BP1 were essentially identical after 30 min, 60 min, or 120 min of exposure to NaAsO2.
source: We observed that the recovery rates of GFP-G3BP1 were essentially identical after 30 min, 60 min, or 120 min of exposure to NaAsO2 (Figure 5), although the half-time of recovery was slightly faster at 30 min (18.5 s) as compared to 60 min (35 s) and 120 min (31 s).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Stress granules formed less efficiently at lower temperatures with a continuing decline in the rate, overall number and size of stress granule formed as the temperature declined from 37°C to 27°C.
source: We observed that stress granules formed less efficiently at lower temperatures with a continuing decline in the rate, overall number and size of stress granule formed as the temperature declined from 37°C to 27°C (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Lower temperatures do not perturb translational inhibition as evidenced by stress-specific induction of eiF2α-phosphorylation to similar levels amongst all the temperatures assessed.
source: Two observations suggest that lower temperatures do not perturb translational inhibition. First, we observe a stress-specific induction of eiF2α-phosphorylation to similar levels amongst all the temperatures assessed (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is a similar extent of translation repression after 20 min of NaAsO2 stress at 30°C as compared to 37°C as shown by polysome profiling.
source: Second, via polysome profiling, we observed a similar extent of translation repression after 20 min of NaAsO2 stress at 30°C as compared to 37°C. (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Once formed at 37°C, stress granules persist at a lower temperature (30°C) and do not appreciably decrease in size.
source: We observed that once formed, stress granules persist at a lower temperature and do not appreciably decrease in size.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Shifting cells to 30°C without NaAsO2 does not induce stress granule formation.
source: It should be noted that shifting cells to 30°C (without NaAsO2) does not induce stress granule formation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The addition of 10% 1,6-Hexanediol to yeast cells rapidly disrupted the nuclear pore, as adjudged by the loss of punctate, peri-nuclear localization of the nuclear pore protein, Nsp1.
source: Consistent with this prediction, the addition of 10% 1,6-Hexanediol to yeast cells (Kroschwald et al., 2015), rapidly disrupted the nuclear pore, as adjudged by the loss of punctate, peri-nuclear localization of the nuclear pore protein, Nsp1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 1,6-Hexanediol caused a significant disruption of actin and tubulin organization in yeast.
source: We observed that 1,6-Hexanediol (but not 1, 4, 6-Hexanetriol) caused a significant disruption of actin and tubulin organization, as adjudged by the localization of Sac6-GFP (an actin binding protein) and Tub1-GFP (Alpha-Tubulin) respectively (Figure 7A and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Disruption of cytoskeleton organization by 1,6-Hexanediol occurred within two minutes of treatment.
source: This disruption of cytoskeleton organization occurred within two minutes of 1,6-Hexanediol treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Membrane bound cellular structures such as the Endoplasmic Reticulum and mitochondria were not affected by 1,6-Hexanediol.
source: Membrane bound cellular structures such as the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER, observed using Get1-GFP) and mitochondria (observed using Atp1-GFP) were not affected by 1,6-Hexanediol.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: HeLa cells demonstrated a 40% reduction in cellular viability following exposure to 3.5% 1,6-Hexanediol as compared to untreated cells.
source: First, HeLa cells demonstrated a 40% reduction in cellular viability as assessed by RealTime-Glo MT Cell Viability Assay following exposure to 3.5% 1,6-Hexanediol as compared to untreated cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: HeLa cells exposed to 1,6-Hexanediol demonstrated rapid widespread morphological changes within seconds including membrane blebbing.
source: Second, HeLa cells exposed to 1,6-Hexanediol demonstrated rapid widespread morphological changes within seconds including membrane blebbing (Figure 7B; Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B and Video 2.

claim: In yeast, both stress granules and P-bodies quickly disassembled within two minutes of 1,6-Hexanediol treatment, but after 10 min, they reappeared, often completely co-localized.
source: First, both assemblies quickly disassembled within two minutes, however, after 10 min, they reappeared, often completely co-localized (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the absence of any other stress, 1,6-Hexanediol induced robust Pab1-GFP (a stress granule marker) granule formation within 10 min of treatment in yeast.
source: By using strains with tagged components of stress granules and P-bodies, we observed that in the absence of any other stress, 1,6-Hexanediol (and not a Digitonin control) also induced robust Pab1-GFP (a stress granule marker) granule formation within 10 min of treatment (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 1,6-Hexanediol-induced Pab1-GFP foci overlapped with Edc3-mCherry, a P-body protein, in yeast.
source: Interestingly, these Pab1-GFP foci also overlapped with Edc3-mCherry – a P-body protein (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In HeLa cells with pre-existing stress granules induced by NaAsO2, 1,6-Hexanediol treatment caused an initial reduction in total stress granule numbers, but after 10 min, stress granules re-appeared.
source: Similar to yeast stress granules, we observed an initial reduction in total stress granule numbers, which coincided with alterations in cellular morphology; however, after 10 min, stress granules re-appeared (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the absence of any other stress, 1,6-Hexanediol treatment resulted in the formation of stress granule-like assemblies in HeLa cells that stained positive for stress granule markers G3BP1 and PABP1.
source: In the absence of any other stress, 1,6-Hexanediol treatment resulted in the formation of stress granule-like assemblies. These assemblies stained positive for stress granule markers G3BP1 and PABP1 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 9B.

claim: 1,6-Hexanediol induces the formation of assemblies that contain known stress granule proteins in both yeast and mammalian cells (HeLa and U-2 OS cells).
source: First, 1,6-Hexanediol induces the formation of assemblies that contain known stress granule proteins in both yeast and mammalian cells (HeLa and U-2 OS cells) (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10A.

claim: 1,6-Hexanediol induced assemblies are sensitive to cycloheximide treatment in both yeast and mammalian cells.
source: Second, 1,6-Hexanediol induced assemblies are sensitive to cycloheximide treatment, a drug known to block stress granule assembly, in both yeast and mammalian cells (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10A.

claim: 1,6-Hexanediol-induced assemblies are stable in lysates.
source: Third, 1,6-Hexanediol-induced assemblies are stable in lysates suggesting that the material properties of these assemblies contain a relatively stable set of interactions similar to normal stress granules (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: eiF2α phosphorylation is induced to a similar extent by 1,6-Hexanediol compared to NaAsO2.
source: Fourth, eiF2α phosphorylation is induced to a similar extent by 1,6-Hexanediol compared to NaAsO2 (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10C.

claim: FRAP analysis of 1,6-Hexanediol-induced granules in mammalian cells indicates that 1,6-Hexanediol induced stress granules behave similar to normal stress granules.
source: Finally, FRAP analysis of 1,6-Hexanediol-induced granules in mammalian cells indicates that 1,6-Hexanediol induced stress granules behave similar to normal stress granules (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 10D.

claim: For large stress granules, disassembly appears to occur in two steps: first, larger stress granules break into smaller foci followed by disassembly and/or clearance of these smaller foci.
source: Within the limitations of our ability to detect stress granule disassembly, we observe for large stress granules, disassembly appears to occur in two steps: first, larger stress granules break into smaller foci followed by disassembly and/or clearance of these smaller foci.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: During disassembly, filamentous structures emerge at the edges of the disassembling stress granule.
source: During disassembly, we observe the appearance of filamentous structures emerging at the edges of the disassembling stress granule; however, we should point out that due to the resolution of our microscope we are unable to characterize the nature of these structures (Figure 11BC).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11B,C.

claim: Examination of stress granule disassembly reveals non-uniform distribution within stress granules undergoing disassembly wherein areas of relative concentration appear to persist once the surrounding shell structures have dissolved.
source: Second, examination of stress granule disassembly reveals non-uniform distribution within stress granules undergoing disassembly wherein areas of relative concentration appear to persist once the surrounding shell structures have dissolved (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Stress granules are stable in lysates at the same time points that disassembly is occurring.
source: Finally, we observe stress granules are stable in lysates at the same time points that disassembly is occurring (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Core assembly represents an early event in stress granule formation.
source: Based on these two observations, we conclude that core assembly represents an early event in stress granule formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the data presented.

claim: The primary driving forces of stress granule assembly are not weak interactions between IDR domains that are enhanced at low temperatures.
source: This suggests that the primary driving forces of stress granule assembly are not weak interactions between IDR domains that are enhanced at low temperatures.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the temperature experiments.

claim: The process of stress granule assembly in cells is not primarily driven by weak, dynamic homo- and heterotypic interactions between IDRs on RNA binding proteins analogous to the LLPS driven by these protein domains in vitro.
source: These observations suggest that the process of stress granule assembly in cells is not primarily driven by weak, dynamic homo- and heterotypic interactions between IDRs on RNA binding proteins analogous to the LLPS driven by these protein domains in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the temperature and 1,6-Hexanediol experiments.

claim: Weak, dynamic interactions between IDRs could be important in forming the shell structure of stress granules, once the core is nucleated by more stable interactions.
source: However, we hypothesize that weak, dynamic interactions between IDRs could be important in forming the shell structure of stress granules, once the core is nucleated by more stable interactions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: The sensitivity of a cellular structure to 1,6-Hexanediol does not appear sufficient to conclude the structure forms by LLPS.
source: In any case, the sensitivity of a cellular structure to 1,6-Hexanediol does not appear sufficient to conclude the structure forms by LLPS.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the 1,6-Hexanediol experiments.

claim: Small stress granules that form early in a stress response require microtubules and their associated motors to form larger stress granules.
source: Previous work has suggested that small stress granules that form early in a stress response require microtubules and their associated motors to form larger stress granules (Chernov et al., 2009; Fujimura et al., 2009; Ivanov et al., 2003; Loschi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Treatment of cells with nocadazole, which depolymerizes microtubules, prevents the fusion of the small initial stress granules into larger assemblies.
source: In those experiments, treatment of cells with nocadazole, which depolymerizes microtubules, prevents the fusion of the small initial stress granules into larger assemblies.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion referring to previous work.

claim: Cores are brought together to form larger assemblies by movement on microtubules.
source: Based on these results, a reasonable model is that cores are brought together to form larger assemblies by movement on microtubules.
evidence: This is a model proposed in the discussion based on previous work.

claim: Upon re-establishment of translation, mRNA is thought to be in rapid equilibrium between the cytosol and stress granules.
source: First, upon re-establishment of translation, mRNA is thought to be in rapid equilibrium between the cytosol and stress granules.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: The lag in the clearance of granule cores may reflect the requirement of a myriad of ATP-dependent remodeling complexes.
source: The lag in the clearance of granule cores may reflect the requirement of a myriad of ATP-dependent remodeling complexes (e.g. heat shock 70 or p97/VCP AAA-ATPase complexes [Buchan et al., 2013; Walters et al., 2015]) and could serve as a cytoprotective mechanism to acutely re-nucleate stress granules if the cell re-encounters stress.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis with supporting citations.

claim: A biphasic stress granule architecture provides multiple layers of functionality within the larger tunable stress-specific RNA transcriptome.
source: In mammalian cells, a biphasic stress granule architecture provides multiple layers of functionality within the larger tunable stress-specific RNA transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: A shell in mammalian cells provides a scaffold for dynamic exchange of select RNAs out of the translational pool.
source: First, a shell in mammalian cells provides a scaffold for dynamic exchange of select RNAs out of the translational pool.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: Hyper-nucleation or inefficient clearance of stress granule cores may facilitate a pathological transition by lowering the free energy landscape to seed an β-amyloid aggregate by providing a continued platform for nucleation.
source: Hyper-nucleation or inefficient clearance of stress granule cores may facilitate a pathological transition by lowering the free energy landscape to seed an β-amyloid aggregate by providing a continued platform for nucleation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis about disease mechanisms.

claim: Stable core structures could provide a structural platform, due to the high concentration of IDRs on stress granule components, to then rapidly phase-separate a dynamic shell.
source: We hypothesize that these stable core assemblies could provide a structural platform, due to the high concentration of IDRs on stress granule components to then rapidly phase-separate a dynamic shell that grows as a result of fusion with other small granules and surface exchange with an increasing pool of untranslating mRNPs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: The oligomerization of individual mRNPs into core structures would be analogous to a liquid-liquid phase separation driven by multivalent interactions.
source: The oligomerization of individual mRNPs into core structures would be analogous to a liquid-liquid phase separation driven by multivalent interactions, but because the core structures are stable to dilution, could be considered a liquid-solid demixing phase separation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: The shell region of stress granules does not persist in lysis conditions, which suggests it is sensitive to dilution, one of the properties of an LLPS.
source: The shell region of stress granules does not persist in our lysis conditions, which suggests it is sensitive to dilution, one of the properties of an LLPS.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the lysis experiments.

claim: Assembly of a mature stress granule occurs via a multistep process: an initial nucleation event that may be influenced by the stress stimulus and a consistent growth phase that requires an addition of substrate and fusion of the small initial stress granules into larger assemblies.
source: Our data is consistent with the idea that assembly of a mature stress granule occurs via a multistep process: an initial nucleation event that may be influenced by the stress stimulus and a consistent growth phase that requires an addition of substrate and fusion of the small initial stress granules into larger assemblies.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the time-course data.

claim: Stress granule disassembly may occur through multiple steps wherein RNA is titrated out of stress granule into translation leading to structural instability and subsequent disassembly of a larger stress granule complex into smaller core structures that are then disassembled or cleared by autophagy.
source: Taken together, stress granule disassembly may occur through multiple steps wherein RNA is titrated out of stress granule into translation leading to structural instability and subsequent disassembly of a larger stress granule complex into smaller core structures that are then disassembled or cleared by autophagy.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the disassembly data.

claim: When the initial step in stress granule assembly is formation of a stable core, the core structure could then provide a high local concentration of IDRs on stress granule components, which could then trigger a local phase separation.
source: When the initial step in stress granule assembly is formation of a stable core, which by definition involves relatively stable interactions, the core structure could then provide a high local concentration of IDRs on stress granule components, which could then be envisioned to trigger a local phase separation, possibly what we refer to as the shell phase of a stress granule.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: The creation of a high local concentration of FG repeat proteins by the structure of the nuclear pore allows for a phase transition within the nuclear pore itself.
source: This general principle is also seen in the formation of the nuclear pore, wherein the creation of a high local concentration of FG repeat proteins by the structure of the nuclear pore, allows for a phase transition within the nuclear pore itself, even if the interactions between the FG repeats are relatively weak and non-specific (Frey and Görlich, 2007; Hülsmann et al., 2012; Schmidt and Görlich, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.
